meta.notes: Level 3 is NCERT-hard: self-constructed, multi-step, but strictly in-syllabus (no JEE-Advanced-style tricks). Bonus questions mix two or more topics from this chapter and are tagged via mixed_topics (internally stored with level: 3); unlock after Level 3 or serve as a standalone challenge round. Topic drill mode: filter questions by topic across all levels, order L1->L2->L3, serve in sets of ~6. Each topic has a concept card in the 'topics' array (summary, key_formulas, worked_example, common_mistakes) shown via a 'See concept' button. Topic names in 'topics' match question 'topic' tags exactly for lookup. After a failed level, link weak topics to their drill + concept card. This chapter is bonding/structure heavy rather than numerical-calculation heavy: dominant distractor patterns are VSEPR shape vs. electron-geometry confusion, hybridisation miscounts, sigma/pi bond miscounts, MO bond-order errors, invalid resonance structures, and formal-charge errors, rather than unit-conversion mistakes.
meta.rendering: All question/option/explanation/hint/concept text uses lightweight HTML, rendered via innerHTML: <sup>/<sub> for charges, formal charges, and formula subscripts (e.g. NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>); δ+ / δ− for partial charges; ° for bond angles; ↔ for resonance structures; → for reactions; σ/π for sigma/pi bond types; Δ where needed; a true minus sign (−, not a hyphen) in all charges, formal charges, and negative values; × for multiplication; μ for dipole moment; ±, ≈, ∝, ≡ where relevant; –/— for en/em dashes. No LaTeX/KaTeX is used in this chapter (unlike the Mathematics bank) since bonding notation is fully expressible in simple HTML entities and tags.

questions.question: According to the octet rule, atoms are most stable when their valence shell contains:
options: 8 electrons
18 electrons
6 electrons
4 electrons
questions.explanation: Kossel and Lewis proposed that atoms tend to combine so as to acquire 8 electrons in their outermost (valence) shell, resembling the nearest noble gas — this is the octet rule.
questions.hint: Think of the electron count of the nearest noble gas (other than helium).
distractor_logic: confuses octet with an expanded shell count
still short of a full octet
too few electrons for a stable octet

questions.question: In a Lewis (electron-dot) structure, a pair of dots placed between two bonded atoms represents:
options: A lone pair on the right atom
A formal charge
A shared (bond) pair of electrons
A lone pair on the left atom
questions.explanation: Dots drawn between two atomic symbols in a Lewis structure represent a bond pair — electrons shared between the two bonded atoms — while dots placed beside a single symbol represent an unshared lone pair.
questions.hint: A pair sitting between two symbols belongs to the bond, not to one atom alone.
distractor_logic: misplaces a shared pair as belonging only to one atom
confuses bond pair notation with formal charge notation
misplaces a shared pair as belonging only to one atom

questions.question: An ionic bond is most favoured between an atom with a ___ ionisation enthalpy and an atom with a ___ (more negative) electron gain enthalpy.
options: high; high
high; low
low; high
low; low
questions.explanation: Ionic bond formation is favoured when one atom loses an electron easily (low ionisation enthalpy, typically a metal) and the other atom gains an electron readily with a large release of energy (high negative electron gain enthalpy, typically a non-metal).
questions.hint: One atom must give up an electron easily; the other must want to take it strongly.
distractor_logic: both conditions reversed
conditions swapped between the two atoms
neither condition favours easy electron transfer

questions.question: The formal charge on an atom in a Lewis structure is calculated as:
options: Valence electrons − bonding electrons only
Non-bonding electrons − bonding electrons
Valence electrons − non-bonding electrons − ½(bonding electrons)
½(valence electrons) − non-bonding electrons
questions.explanation: Formal charge = (valence electrons of the free atom) − (non-bonding electrons on it in the structure) − ½(bonding electrons around it). This is the standard NCERT definition.
questions.hint: Remember to only take half of the bonding electrons, not all of them.
distractor_logic: omits the non-bonding electron term entirely
swaps which terms get subtracted
omits the bonding electron contribution

questions.question: For any Lewis structure of a molecule or ion, the sum of the formal charges on all its atoms must equal:
options: The number of bonds in the structure
The total number of valence electrons
Zero, always
The overall charge on the species
questions.explanation: By definition, formal charges are a way of redistributing the overall charge among the atoms of a structure, so they must always add up to the actual net charge on the whole species (zero for a neutral molecule, or the ion's charge for an ion).
questions.hint: For a neutral molecule this happens to be zero, but is that true for an ion too?
distractor_logic: unrelated to what formal charges represent
not a meaningful quantity to sum to
only true for neutral molecules, not the general rule

questions.question: Lattice enthalpy of an ionic solid is best described as the energy:
options: Released when the ionic solid dissolves in water
Required to melt one mole of the ionic solid
Released when gaseous ions combine to form one mole of the ionic solid
Required to ionise one mole of the gaseous metal atoms
questions.explanation: Lattice enthalpy is the energy released when the requisite number of gaseous cations and anions combine to form one mole of the solid crystalline ionic compound.
questions.hint: Think in terms of gaseous ions coming together, not melting or dissolving.
distractor_logic: confuses it with enthalpy of solution
confuses lattice enthalpy with enthalpy of fusion
confuses it with ionisation enthalpy

questions.question: Which combination of properties most favours the formation of an ionic bond between atoms A and B?
options: A has high ionisation enthalpy, B has low electron gain enthalpy
Both A and B have high ionisation enthalpy
Both A and B have low electron gain enthalpy
A has low ionisation enthalpy, B has high (negative) electron gain enthalpy
questions.explanation: Ionic bonding is favoured when one atom (A) loses an electron easily (low ionisation enthalpy) and the other (B) gains an electron with a large release of energy (high negative electron gain enthalpy).
questions.hint: One atom should give an electron away easily; the other should want to accept it strongly.
distractor_logic: makes electron loss from A difficult
makes both atoms reluctant to lose or gain an electron appropriately
makes electron gain by B unfavourable

questions.question: A characteristic general property of ionic compounds is that they:
options: Are typically soft and malleable solids
Conduct electricity when molten or in aqueous solution, due to mobile ions
Have low melting points and are usually liquids at room temperature
Conduct electricity in the solid state but not when molten
questions.explanation: Ionic compounds form rigid crystal lattices with high melting points; the ions are fixed in place in the solid but become mobile (and hence able to conduct electricity) once molten or dissolved in water.
questions.hint: Electrical conduction by ions needs the ions to be free to move.
distractor_logic: wrongly assigns softness/malleability, a metallic-bonding property
wrongly assigns low mp/liquid state to ionic compounds
reverses the correct conducting condition

questions.question: Bond length is defined as:
options: The equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms
The angle between two bonds at a central atom
The number of bonds between two atoms
The energy required to break a bond
questions.explanation: Bond length is the equilibrium (average) distance between the nuclei of two atoms directly bonded to each other, usually expressed in picometres (pm).
questions.hint: It is a distance, not an energy or an angle.
distractor_logic: describes bond angle instead
describes bond order instead
describes bond enthalpy instead

questions.question: Bond enthalpy is the energy:
options: Released when one mole of a solid ionic compound forms
Required to move an electron from the valence shell to infinity
Released when a molecule condenses from gas to liquid
Required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state
questions.explanation: Bond enthalpy is the amount of energy needed to break one mole of a specific covalent bond between two atoms in the gaseous state, yielding separated gaseous atoms.
questions.hint: It concerns breaking a specific covalent bond, atom to atom.
distractor_logic: describes lattice enthalpy instead
describes ionisation enthalpy instead
describes enthalpy of condensation instead

questions.question: Bond order is defined as the:
options: Number of bonds (σ + π) between two bonded atoms
Angle subtended by two bonds at a central atom
Distance between two bonded nuclei
Energy needed to break a bond
questions.explanation: Bond order is simply the total number of bonds — the sum of sigma and pi bonds — that exist between a given pair of bonded atoms, e.g. a double bond has bond order 2.
questions.hint: A single bond has order 1, a double bond has order 2 — what is being counted?
distractor_logic: describes bond angle instead
describes bond length instead
describes bond enthalpy instead

questions.question: Bond length is most commonly expressed in the unit:
options: Picometre (pm)
Debye
Joule
Coulomb
questions.explanation: Bond length, a distance between two nuclei, is expressed in picometres (pm) or angstroms (Å); joule measures energy, Debye measures dipole moment, and coulomb measures electric charge.
questions.hint: Think distance, not energy, dipole, or charge.
distractor_logic: a unit of dipole moment, not distance
a unit of energy, not distance
a unit of electric charge, not distance

questions.question: Resonance is best described as a situation where:
options: Two or more valid Lewis structures (differing only in electron placement) together describe one real, intermediate structure
The molecule has no valid Lewis structure at all
The molecule physically oscillates rapidly between two or more structures
A single Lewis structure accurately shows all bonding in the molecule
questions.explanation: When more than one valid Lewis structure (with the same atomic positions but different electron arrangements) can be drawn, none of them alone is correct; the real molecule is a single resonance hybrid, intermediate in character between the contributing structures — it does not flip between them.
questions.hint: The molecule does not switch between forms; it is genuinely one hybrid structure.
distractor_logic: incorrectly claims no Lewis structure can be drawn
the classic misconception that resonance is oscillation
opposite of resonance — a single structure being sufficient

questions.question: The actual structure of a molecule showing resonance, intermediate between its contributing (canonical) structures, is called the:
options: Excited state
Transition state
Resonance hybrid
Ground state configuration
questions.explanation: The single real structure of a resonating molecule, which is intermediate in energy and bonding character between all its valid contributing (canonical) structures, is called the resonance hybrid.
questions.hint: This term specifically describes the 'blend' of the contributing structures.
distractor_logic: an electronic excitation term, unrelated to resonance
a kinetics term, unrelated to resonance
describes the lowest-energy electron arrangement, not the hybrid concept

questions.question: For two Lewis structures to be valid resonance structures of the same species, they must have:
options: Different total numbers of valence electrons
The same positions of all atoms, with only electron (bond/lone pair) positions differing
Different molecular formulas
Different positions of all atoms but the same electrons
questions.explanation: Valid resonance structures keep every atom in exactly the same position; only the arrangement of bonding and lone pair electrons is allowed to differ between them.
questions.hint: What is allowed to move between resonance structures — atoms, or electrons?
distractor_logic: would mean they aren't even the same species
describes different compounds, not resonance structures of one species
reverses what is allowed to move (atoms instead of electrons)

questions.topic: Polarity of Bonds and Dipole Moment
questions.question: Dipole moment (μ) of a bond is defined as the product of:
options: Number of lone pairs and bond angle
Electronegativity difference and bond enthalpy
The magnitude of charge separated and the distance between the charge centres
Bond order and bond length
questions.explanation: Dipole moment μ = q × d, the product of the magnitude of the separated charge (q) and the distance (d) between the centres of positive and negative charge.
questions.hint: It's charge times distance, exactly as the formula μ = q × d suggests.
distractor_logic: not the defining formula for dipole moment
not the defining formula for dipole moment
mixes up bond order/length, unrelated quantities

questions.topic: Polarity of Bonds and Dipole Moment
questions.question: The SI-adjacent unit conventionally used to express dipole moment is the:
options: Tesla (T)
Pascal (Pa)
Farad (F)
Debye (D)
questions.explanation: Dipole moments are conventionally expressed in Debye (D), a unit sized conveniently for molecular dipole moments (1 D = 3.33564 × 10<sup>−30</sup> C m).
questions.hint: This unit is named after the physicist who pioneered dipole moment measurements.
distractor_logic: a unit of magnetic flux density, unrelated to dipole moment
a unit of pressure, unrelated to dipole moment
a unit of capacitance, unrelated to dipole moment

questions.topic: Polarity of Bonds and Dipole Moment
questions.question: Dipole moment is a:
options: Scalar quantity with magnitude only
Dimensionless ratio
Vector quantity, having both magnitude and direction
Quantity that only applies to ionic compounds
questions.explanation: Dipole moment is a vector quantity; it has both a magnitude and a direction, conventionally represented as pointing from the positive end of the dipole to the negative end.
questions.hint: Since bond dipoles must be added considering direction, what kind of quantity must dipole moment be?
distractor_logic: ignores its directional character, which is essential for vector addition in polyatomic molecules
it carries real physical units (Debye), not a dimensionless ratio
dipole moment is a property of polar covalent bonds too, not only ionic ones

questions.question: According to Fajans' rules, covalent character in an ionic bond increases as the size of the cation:
options: Has no effect on covalent character
Increases
Becomes equal to the anion's size
Decreases
questions.explanation: A smaller cation has a higher charge density and therefore polarises the anion's electron cloud more strongly, increasing the covalent character of the bond (Fajans' rules).
questions.hint: A smaller, more concentrated positive charge pulls harder on the anion's electrons.
distractor_logic: denies the well-established size effect
states the opposite trend
not what Fajans' rules state

questions.question: According to Fajans' rules, covalent character in an ionic bond increases as the size of the anion:
options: Becomes equal to the cation's size
Has no effect on covalent character
Increases
Decreases
questions.explanation: A larger anion has a more diffuse, loosely held electron cloud that is more easily polarised (distorted) by the cation, increasing covalent character of the bond (Fajans' rules).
questions.hint: A bigger, more diffuse electron cloud is easier for the cation to distort.
distractor_logic: not what Fajans' rules state
denies the well-established size effect
states the opposite trend for the anion

questions.question: VSEPR stands for:
options: Variable Shell Electron Pair Repulsion
Valence Shared Electron Pair Reaction
Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion
Valence Shell Energy Pair Resonance
questions.explanation: VSEPR is the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory, used to predict molecular shapes based on minimising repulsion among electron pairs around a central atom.
questions.hint: Break the acronym down letter by letter.
distractor_logic: wrong words for 'Variable' and 'Repulsion'
wrong words for 'Shared' and 'Reaction'
wrong word for the second and fourth letters

questions.question: The basic postulate of VSEPR theory is that electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves to:
options: Maximise their mutual repulsion
Align themselves in a single fixed straight line regardless of number
Overlap with each other as much as possible
Minimise their mutual repulsion by staying as far apart as possible
questions.explanation: VSEPR theory states that electron pairs (bonding and lone) around a central atom repel one another and therefore arrange themselves in space to be as far apart as possible, minimising overall repulsion.
questions.hint: Think of electron pairs as trying to get away from each other, not closer.
distractor_logic: states the opposite goal (maximising repulsion)
ignores that the arrangement depends on the number of electron pairs present
confuses electron pair arrangement with orbital overlap in bonding

questions.question: The correct order of repulsive strength between electron pairs, from strongest to weakest, is:
options: All three types of repulsion are equal in strength
lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair
lone pair–bond pair > lone pair–lone pair > bond pair–bond pair
bond pair–bond pair > lone pair–bond pair > lone pair–lone pair
questions.explanation: Lone pairs, being held closer to the nucleus by only one atom, occupy more space and repel more strongly than bond pairs; the correct order is lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.
questions.hint: Lone pairs take up more space than bond pairs, which are 'stretched' between two nuclei.
distractor_logic: wrongly claims all repulsions are equal, ignoring bond angle compression trends
places lone pair-bond pair repulsion incorrectly as strongest
reverses the entire order

questions.question: According to VSEPR theory, the shape of CH<sub>4</sub>, with 4 bond pairs and no lone pairs on carbon, is:
options: Square planar
Trigonal planar
Tetrahedral
Trigonal pyramidal
questions.explanation: With 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs on the central carbon, the 4 C−H bonds arrange themselves in a tetrahedral geometry to minimise repulsion, giving the familiar tetrahedral shape of methane with 109.5° bond angles.
questions.hint: Four bond pairs, zero lone pairs — the classic methane shape.
distractor_logic: the shape for 4 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs (steric number 6)
the shape for 3 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs (steric number 3)
the shape for 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair, not 4 bond pairs + 0 lone pairs

questions.question: A sigma (σ) bond is formed by:
options: Overlap of orbitals at 90° to each other
No orbital overlap at all
Head-on (axial) overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis
Sideways (lateral) overlap of parallel p orbitals
questions.explanation: A sigma bond forms by head-on (axial) overlap of atomic or hybrid orbitals directly along the line joining the two nuclei (the internuclear axis).
questions.hint: Picture two orbitals approaching each other straight on, along the bond axis.
distractor_logic: orbitals at 90° give zero net overlap, not a sigma bond
no overlap means no covalent bond forms at all
describes pi bond formation instead

questions.question: A pi (π) bond is formed by:
options: Sideways (lateral) overlap of unhybridised p orbitals lying parallel to each other
Overlap of two hybrid orbitals along the bond axis
Complete transfer of an electron from one atom to another
Head-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis
questions.explanation: A pi bond forms by sideways (lateral) overlap of unhybridised p orbitals that lie parallel to each other and perpendicular to the internuclear axis, above and below (or in front of/behind) the sigma bond.
questions.hint: Picture two p orbitals lying side by side, overlapping sideways rather than head-on.
distractor_logic: head-on hybrid orbital overlap describes a sigma bond, not a pi bond
describes ionic bond formation, not a pi bond
describes sigma bond formation instead

questions.question: Between a sigma bond and a pi bond formed by the same pair of atoms, which is generally stronger?
options: Both are always exactly equal in strength
The sigma bond, because head-on overlap is more effective than sideways overlap
The pi bond, because it is drawn as an 'extra' line
Neither has any bond strength; only ionic bonds have strength
questions.explanation: Head-on (axial) overlap in a sigma bond is more extensive and effective than the sideways (lateral) overlap in a pi bond, making sigma bonds generally stronger than pi bonds between the same atoms.
questions.hint: Which type of overlap brings orbital density more directly between the two nuclei?
distractor_logic: ignores the real difference in overlap effectiveness
a common misconception; being 'extra' does not make it stronger
covalent bonds, both sigma and pi, clearly have bond strength/enthalpy

questions.question: Hybridisation is the process of:
options: Mixing atomic orbitals of comparable energy on the same atom to form a new set of equivalent orbitals
Splitting a single atomic orbital into two separate atoms
Forming ionic bonds between two non-metal atoms
Transferring electrons completely from one atom to another
questions.explanation: Hybridisation is the intermixing of atomic orbitals of similar energy belonging to the same atom, producing a new set of equivalent hybrid orbitals suitable for bond formation, matching observed molecular shapes.
questions.hint: It happens within one atom, mixing its own orbitals together.
distractor_logic: hybridisation combines orbitals, it doesn't split one into separate atoms
hybridisation is an orbital-mixing concept, not specifically about ionic bonding
describes ionic bond formation, not hybridisation

questions.question: sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation involves the mixing of:
options: One s and three p orbitals
One s, one p, and one d orbital
One s and two p orbitals
Three s orbitals
questions.explanation: sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation mixes one s orbital and three p orbitals from the same atom, producing four equivalent sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally.
questions.hint: Count the superscripts: s<sup>1</sup>p<sup>3</sup> means how many of each orbital?
distractor_logic: this describes sp<sup>3</sup>d, which needs a d orbital too
this combination is sp<sup>2</sup>, not sp<sup>3</sup>
s orbitals cannot combine only with other s orbitals to give directional hybrid orbitals

questions.question: The number of hybrid orbitals produced by sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation is:
questions.explanation: sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation mixes 1 s orbital and 2 p orbitals, and the total number of atomic orbitals mixed always equals the number of hybrid orbitals produced — giving 3 equivalent sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals.
questions.hint: Add up the orbitals being mixed: 1 (s) + 2 (p).
distractor_logic: this is the count for sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation
this is the count for sp<sup>3</sup>d hybridisation
this is the count for sp hybridisation

questions.question: In methane (CH<sub>4</sub>), the hybridisation of the central carbon atom is:
options: sp<sup>3</sup>
sp
sp<sup>2</sup>
sp<sup>3</sup>d
questions.explanation: Carbon in CH<sub>4</sub> forms 4 sigma bonds with no lone pairs (steric number 4), which corresponds to sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation and a tetrahedral shape.
questions.hint: Count carbon's steric number in methane: 4 bonded atoms, 0 lone pairs.
distractor_logic: the hybridisation for steric number 2
the hybridisation for steric number 3
the hybridisation for steric number 5, not 4

questions.question: Molecular Orbital Theory was mainly developed by:
options: Heisenberg and Schrodinger
Hund and Mulliken
Pauling and Slater
Lewis and Kossel
questions.explanation: Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT) was developed principally by F. Hund and R. S. Mulliken, describing electrons in a molecule as occupying molecular orbitals formed by combining atomic orbitals.
questions.hint: These two scientists' names are directly linked with molecular orbital theory in NCERT.
distractor_logic: these two are associated with quantum mechanics generally, not specifically MOT
these are associated with valence bond theory/hybridisation, not MOT
these two proposed the Lewis/octet approach, not MOT

questions.question: In Molecular Orbital Theory, a bonding molecular orbital, compared to the atomic orbitals that combined to form it, has:
options: No defined energy
Higher energy
Lower energy
Exactly the same energy
questions.explanation: A bonding molecular orbital results from the in-phase (additive) combination of atomic orbitals and has lower energy than the original atomic orbitals, stabilising the molecule when occupied by electrons.
questions.hint: 'Bonding' orbitals stabilise the molecule — so is their energy raised or lowered?
distractor_logic: molecular orbitals have well-defined energies, just like atomic orbitals
this describes the antibonding MO, not the bonding MO
the two combining orbitals must produce a stabilised (lower) and destabilised (higher) MO, not equal energies

questions.question: In Molecular Orbital Theory, bond order is calculated using the formula:
options: N<sub>b</sub> − N<sub>a</sub>
(N<sub>b</sub> − N<sub>a</sub>)/2
(N<sub>b</sub> + N<sub>a</sub>)/2
N<sub>b</sub> × N<sub>a</sub>
questions.explanation: Bond order in MOT is calculated as half the difference between the number of electrons in bonding molecular orbitals (N<sub>b</sub>) and antibonding molecular orbitals (N<sub>a</sub>): Bond order = (N<sub>b</sub> − N<sub>a</sub>)/2.
questions.hint: It's half the difference, not the sum, of bonding and antibonding electrons.
distractor_logic: forgets to divide the difference by 2
adds instead of subtracting the electron counts
multiplies instead of using the correct subtraction/division formula

questions.question: LCAO, the method used to construct molecular orbitals, stands for:
options: Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals
Linear Configuration of Atomic Order
Localised Combination of Anti-bonding Orbitals
Lowest Combination of Atomic Orbitals
questions.explanation: LCAO stands for Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals — molecular orbitals are constructed mathematically by adding or subtracting the wave functions of combining atomic orbitals.
questions.hint: Break the acronym down: Linear ___ of Atomic Orbitals.
distractor_logic: not the correct expansion of LCAO
not the correct expansion of LCAO
wrong word for 'Linear'

questions.question: Using Molecular Orbital Theory, the bond order of the N<sub>2</sub> molecule is:
questions.explanation: N<sub>2</sub> has 10 valence electrons giving 8 bonding and 2 antibonding electrons, so bond order = (8−2)/2 = 3, consistent with its well-known triple bond (N≡N) and very high bond enthalpy.
questions.hint: N<sub>2</sub> is famous for having a triple bond — what bond order does a triple bond represent?
distractor_logic: too high; N<sub>2</sub> does not have a quadruple bond
too low for N<sub>2</sub>'s known triple bond
too low for N<sub>2</sub>'s known triple bond

questions.question: Which of these homonuclear diatomic species does NOT exist as a stable molecule, because Molecular Orbital Theory predicts a bond order of zero?
options: He<sub>2</sub>
N<sub>2</sub>
H<sub>2</sub>
O<sub>2</sub>
questions.explanation: He<sub>2</sub> would have equal numbers of bonding and antibonding electrons (2 each), giving bond order (2−2)/2 = 0, so it does not exist as a stable molecule — unlike H<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub>, and O<sub>2</sub>, all of which have positive bond orders and are well-known stable molecules.
questions.hint: Which of these noble-gas-like species has a fully filled bonding AND fully filled antibonding orbital?
distractor_logic: N<sub>2</sub> has bond order 3 and is very stable
H<sub>2</sub> has bond order 1 and is stable
O<sub>2</sub> has bond order 2 and is stable

questions.question: Molecular Orbital Theory correctly predicts that the O<sub>2</sub> molecule is:
options: Paramagnetic, due to two unpaired electrons in antibonding π* orbitals
Diamagnetic, with all electrons paired
Non-existent as a stable species
Ionic in character
questions.explanation: MOT shows that O<sub>2</sub>'s two π*2p orbitals each hold one unpaired electron (by Hund's rule), making O<sub>2</sub> paramagnetic — a property that simple Lewis structures fail to explain but that is experimentally confirmed (liquid O<sub>2</sub> is attracted to a magnet).
questions.hint: This is one of MOT's most celebrated successes over the simple Lewis picture of O=O.
distractor_logic: the opposite of O<sub>2</sub>'s actual, experimentally verified magnetic behaviour
O<sub>2</sub> has bond order 2 and is a well-known stable diatomic gas
O<sub>2</sub> is a covalent molecule between two identical atoms, not ionic

questions.question: A hydrogen bond can form when a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to which type of atom?
options: A small, highly electronegative atom such as F, O, or N
Any metal atom
Any non-metal atom
A large atom of low electronegativity such as S or P
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding requires H to be covalently bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom — specifically F, O or N — which pulls electron density away from H strongly enough to let it interact with a lone pair on a nearby electronegative atom.
questions.hint: Only three elements are small and electronegative enough for this: think F, O, N.
distractor_logic: opposite of the requirement; H-bonding needs non-metals, not metals
too broad; most non-metals (e.g. S, P) do not support significant H-bonding
these atoms are too large/insufficiently electronegative to support significant H-bonding

questions.question: Among HF, HCl, HBr and HI, the compound capable of the strongest hydrogen bonding is:
options: HCl
HI
HBr
HF
questions.explanation: Fluorine is the smallest and most electronegative halogen, so HF forms the strongest hydrogen bonds among the hydrogen halides; Cl, Br and I are all too large and insufficiently electronegative to support significant hydrogen bonding.
questions.hint: Which halogen is smallest and most electronegative?
distractor_logic: Cl is larger and less electronegative than F, so its H-bonding is negligible
I is the largest and least electronegative halogen listed
Br is even larger/less electronegative than Cl

questions.question: BF<sub>3</sub> has only 6 electrons (3 bond pairs) around boron in its Lewis structure. This molecule is best described as an example of:
options: The normal octet rule being obeyed
Odd-electron species
Incomplete octet (electron deficiency)
Expanded octet
questions.explanation: Boron has only 3 valence electrons, so even after forming 3 B−F bonds it has just 6 electrons around it, short of a full octet — this is the incomplete octet (electron-deficient) exception to the octet rule, seen also in BeCl<sub>2</sub>.
questions.hint: Count the electrons around B: 3 bond pairs × 2 = 6, not 8.
distractor_logic: boron clearly does not have a full octet here
BF<sub>3</sub> has an even number of electrons on every atom, not an odd-electron case
expanded octet means MORE than 8 electrons, the opposite of what's happening here

questions.question: What is the formal charge on the central O atom in the structure H−O−H (water), where O has 2 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs?
options: −1
questions.explanation: Oxygen: V = 6, non-bonding electrons N = 4 (2 lone pairs), bonding electrons B = 4 (2 bond pairs). Formal charge = 6 − 4 − 4/2 = 6 − 4 − 2 = 0.
questions.hint: Plug O's values into FC = V − N − B/2: V=6, N=4, B=4.
distractor_logic: would require an unrealistic electron count around neutral water's oxygen

Both isomers should have identical boiling points and solubility, since they have the same molecular formula
Ortho-nitrophenol forms stronger INTERmolecular hydrogen bonds than para-nitrophenol

Ortho-nitrophenol forms a strong INTRAmolecular hydrogen bond (the −OH and adjacent −NO<sub>2</sub> group are close enough to bond with each other within the same molecule), which satisfies its H-bonding capacity internally and prevents it from forming INTERmolecular H-bonds/associating with other molecules or with water, unlike the para isomer
questions.explanation: In ortho-nitrophenol, the −OH and −NO<sub>2</sub> groups are positioned close enough (on adjacent ring carbons) to hydrogen-bond with EACH OTHER within the same molecule (intramolecular H-bonding), which 'uses up' the H-bonding capacity internally, so the molecule doesn't associate with other molecules via intermolecular H-bonding and remains more volatile with lower water solubility; in para-nitrophenol, the groups are too far apart for intramolecular bonding, so they form intermolecular H-bonds instead, causing association, raising the boiling point, and increasing water solubility via H-bonding with water molecules.
questions.hint: Ring position determines whether the two groups can reach each other WITHIN one molecule (ortho) or must instead bond BETWEEN separate molecules (para).
distractor_logic: both isomers have the same functional groups (-OH, -NO<sub>2</sub>) capable of hydrogen bonding; the difference lies in intra- vs intermolecular bonding, not presence/absence of capacity
having identical molecular formula does not guarantee identical physical properties when intramolecular versus intermolecular bonding patterns differ this much
this reverses which isomer favours intermolecular bonding/association; para-, not ortho-, is the one that associates intermolecularly

questions.question: Formic acid (HCOOH) vapour is found to exist substantially as dimers (two molecules joined by a pair of hydrogen bonds), giving it an effective molecular mass roughly double its formula mass in certain vapour-phase measurements. Combine hydrogen bonding concepts with basic bond-parameter/molecular mass reasoning to explain this observation.
options: Vapour density measurements are always inaccurate and this result should be disregarded
The doubled molecular mass indicates that formic acid always exists as a covalent dimer connected by full covalent bonds, not hydrogen bonds
Formic acid cannot hydrogen bond at all, so the doubled mass must be due to an unrelated chemical reaction

Each formic acid molecule has an −OH group (donor) and a C=O group with lone pairs (acceptor); two molecules can align so that each −OH hydrogen-bonds to the other molecule's C=O oxygen, forming a stable, cyclic dimer held together by 2 hydrogen bonds, which behaves as a single unit of roughly double the mass in vapour-phase measurements
questions.explanation: Formic acid has both an H-bond donor (the acidic −OH hydrogen) and an H-bond acceptor (lone pairs on the carbonyl oxygen); two molecules can pair up so that each molecule's −OH hydrogen bonds to the other's C=O oxygen, forming a stable, cyclic dimer held together by 2 hydrogen bonds simultaneously — this dimer behaves as a single kinetic/mass unit in the vapour phase, explaining the observed effective molecular mass close to double the single-molecule formula mass, a classic and well-documented example of hydrogen-bonding-driven association.
questions.hint: Formic acid has BOTH a hydrogen bond donor (-OH) and acceptor (C=O) group, allowing two molecules to bond to EACH OTHER, not just to themselves.
distractor_logic: this is a genuine, well-documented physical chemistry observation (formic acid vapour dimerisation), not a measurement artefact to be dismissed
the association here is specifically through (weaker, non-covalent) hydrogen bonds, not full covalent bonding between the two molecules
formic acid's -OH and C=O groups are exactly the donor/acceptor combination needed for hydrogen bonding; it is well known to hydrogen bond

questions.question: Compare the trends: H<sub>2</sub>O has a much higher boiling point than H<sub>2</sub>S (anomalous, due to hydrogen bonding), while going from H<sub>2</sub>S to H<sub>2</sub>Se to H<sub>2</sub>Te, boiling point increases smoothly (normal trend, following increasing molecular mass/van der Waals forces, no hydrogen bonding). Combine hydrogen-bonding and general intermolecular-force reasoning to explain why H<sub>2</sub>O breaks the pattern but H<sub>2</sub>S, H<sub>2</sub>Se, and H<sub>2</sub>Te follow a normal one.
options: Oxygen is small and highly electronegative enough to support strong hydrogen bonding in H<sub>2</sub>O, an intermolecular force much stronger than the van der Waals forces alone that govern H<sub>2</sub>S/H<sub>2</sub>Se/H<sub>2</sub>Te (whose central atoms, S/Se/Te, are all too large and insufficiently electronegative for significant hydrogen bonding), so only H<sub>2</sub>O shows the anomalous boiling point spike while the other three simply follow the expected mass-driven van der Waals trend among themselves
All four hydrides should show identical hydrogen bonding capability, since they are all group 16 hydrides
H<sub>2</sub>O's high boiling point is due to van der Waals forces alone, unrelated to hydrogen bonding
H<sub>2</sub>S, H<sub>2</sub>Se, and H<sub>2</sub>Te should also show anomalously high boiling points, just like H<sub>2</sub>O
questions.explanation: Oxygen's small size and high electronegativity uniquely qualify it (among group 16 elements) to support strong hydrogen bonding in H<sub>2</sub>O, adding a powerful extra intermolecular attraction on top of ordinary van der Waals forces and driving its boiling point well above the simple mass-based trend; sulfur, selenium, and tellurium are all too large and insufficiently electronegative to support meaningful hydrogen bonding, so H<sub>2</sub>S, H<sub>2</sub>Se, and H<sub>2</sub>Te rely on van der Waals forces alone, which DO increase smoothly and predictably with increasing molecular mass down this sub-series, exactly as observed.
questions.hint: Only the SMALLEST, MOST electronegative member of the group (O) qualifies for significant hydrogen bonding; the larger S/Se/Te members are left with only the 'normal' mass-driven trend among themselves.
distractor_logic: only oxygen, not sulfur/selenium/tellurium, is small and electronegative enough for significant hydrogen bonding; this option wrongly extends that capability to all four
H<sub>2</sub>O's anomalously HIGH boiling point (well above the van der Waals-only trend) is specifically attributed to the EXTRA effect of hydrogen bonding, not to van der Waals forces alone
S, Se, and Te are all too large/insufficiently electronegative for significant hydrogen bonding, which is exactly why only H<sub>2</sub>O (not the other three) shows the anomalous spike

topics.name: Kossel-Lewis Approach and Lewis Structures
topics.summary: The Kössel-Lewis approach explains bond formation through the octet rule: atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons so that each attains 8 electrons (a noble-gas-like configuration) in its valence shell. A Lewis (electron-dot) structure shows valence electrons as dots around the atomic symbol, with shared pairs (bond pairs) drawn between bonded atoms and unshared pairs (lone pairs) kept on individual atoms. To draw one: count total valence electrons, connect atoms with single bonds, complete octets with lone pairs, and convert lone pairs to multiple bonds if any atom is short of an octet. The rule works well for many molecules but has genuine exceptions taught in NCERT: incomplete octets (BF<sub>3</sub>, BeCl<sub>2</sub>), odd-electron species (NO, NO<sub>2</sub>), and expanded octets where a central atom from period 3 or beyond uses vacant d orbitals to hold more than 8 electrons (PCl<sub>5</sub>, SF<sub>6</sub>).
key_formulas: Total valence electrons = Σ(group number contributions of all atoms) ± charge
Octet satisfied when an atom is surrounded by 4 electron pairs (8 electrons)
topics.worked_example: Draw the Lewis structure of CO<sub>2</sub>. Total valence electrons = 4 (C) + 2×6 (O) = 16. Placing C in the centre with single bonds to each O uses 4 electrons and leaves each O one electron short of an octet, so one lone pair on each O is converted into a second bond: O=C=O. Final structure has 2 C=O double bonds and 2 lone pairs on each O, using all 16 electrons with every atom's octet satisfied.
common_mistakes: Assuming every atom must strictly obey the octet rule and missing genuine exceptions like BF<sub>3</sub> or SF<sub>6</sub>
Forgetting to adjust for overall ionic charge while counting total valence electrons
Leaving an atom electron-deficient instead of converting a lone pair into an extra bond

topics.name: Formal Charge
topics.summary: Formal charge is a bookkeeping tool used to judge which of several possible Lewis structures for a molecule or ion is the most reasonable one. It is calculated as: formal charge = (valence electrons of free atom) − (non-bonding electrons on that atom in the structure) − ½(bonding electrons around that atom). The sum of formal charges on all atoms must equal the overall charge on the species. Among competing Lewis structures for the same molecule, the one with formal charges closest to zero, and with any negative formal charge placed on the more electronegative atom, is preferred as the more stable (major) structure. Formal charge is a formalism for comparing structures, not the actual charge distribution, but it correctly predicts, for example, that carbon carries a formal −1 and oxygen a formal +1 in the accepted Lewis structure of CO.
key_formulas: Formal charge = V − N − B/2 (V = valence e<sup>−</sup>, N = non-bonding e<sup>−</sup>, B = bonding e<sup>−</sup>)
Σ(formal charges on all atoms) = overall charge on the species
topics.worked_example: Find the formal charge on N in NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>. Nitrogen has V = 5, it has no lone pair so N = 0, and it shares 4 bond pairs so B = 8. Formal charge = 5 − 0 − 8/2 = +1. Each H has V = 1, N = 0, B = 2, giving formal charge = 1 − 0 − 1 = 0. Total = +1, matching the overall charge on the ion.
common_mistakes: Dividing the total bonding electrons on the whole molecule instead of only those around the one atom being checked
Forgetting to halve the bonding electron count (using B instead of B/2)
Confusing formal charge with actual ionic charge or oxidation number

topics.name: Ionic Bonding and Lattice Enthalpy
topics.summary: An ionic (electrovalent) bond forms by complete transfer of one or more electrons from a metal atom of low ionisation enthalpy to a non-metal atom of high negative electron gain enthalpy, producing oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction in a crystal lattice. Formation is favoured by low ionisation enthalpy of the cation-forming atom, high (negative) electron gain enthalpy of the anion-forming atom, and high lattice enthalpy of the resulting solid, which is the energy released when gaseous ions come together to form one mole of the solid crystal. Lattice enthalpy increases with higher ionic charges and decreases with increasing ionic radii, since electrostatic attraction is proportional to charge product and inversely related to inter-ionic distance. Ionic compounds are typically hard, brittle solids with high melting points that conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved, since ions are mobile only in those states.
key_formulas: Lattice enthalpy ∝ (charge on cation × charge on anion) / (inter-ionic distance)
Ionic bond favoured by: low ionisation enthalpy (metal) + high electron gain enthalpy (non-metal) + high lattice enthalpy
topics.worked_example: Compare the lattice enthalpies of NaCl and MgO. Mg<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup> each carry twice the charge of Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>, and the ionic radii are comparable, so the charge product (2×2 = 4) in MgO greatly exceeds that of NaCl (1×1 = 1). MgO therefore has a much higher lattice enthalpy and a correspondingly much higher melting point than NaCl.
common_mistakes: Assuming smaller ionic radius always dominates over ionic charge when comparing lattice enthalpies
Mixing up ionisation enthalpy (needed to form the cation) with electron gain enthalpy (needed to form the anion)
Thinking ionic solids conduct electricity in the solid state

topics.name: Bond Parameters
topics.summary: Bond parameters describe the physical characteristics of a covalent bond. Bond length is the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms, measured in picometres; it decreases as bond multiplicity increases (C−C > C=C > C≡C) and also decreases as the percentage s-character of the hybrid orbitals used increases (sp < sp<sup>2</sup> < sp<sup>3</sup> bond length, i.e. more s-character gives a shorter, stronger bond). Bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond in the gaseous state and generally increases as bond order increases. Bond order is the number of bonds (σ + π) between two bonded atoms; higher bond order means shorter bond length and higher bond enthalpy. Bond angle is the angle between two adjacent bonds at a central atom, fixed by the geometry of its orbitals and modified by lone-pair repulsions.
key_formulas: Bond order ↑ ⇒ bond length ↓ and bond enthalpy ↑
%s-character ↑ ⇒ bond length ↓ (sp3 > sp2 > sp bond length)
topics.worked_example: Rank C−C, C=C and C≡C by bond length and bond enthalpy. Bond order rises from 1 to 2 to 3 across this series, so bond length falls in the order C−C (154 pm) > C=C (134 pm) > C≡C (120 pm), while bond enthalpy rises in the reverse order, C−C (348 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>) < C=C (614 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>) < C≡C (839 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>).
common_mistakes: Thinking a double bond is simply 'twice as strong' rather than checking the actual bond-order/length/enthalpy relationship
Ignoring the effect of hybridisation (s-character) on bond length when comparing bonds of the same order
Confusing bond order (count of σ+π bonds) with formal charge or oxidation state

topics.name: Resonance
topics.summary: Some molecules and ions cannot be represented accurately by a single Lewis structure because more than one arrangement of electrons (with the atoms held fixed in place) is equally valid; these individual structures are called canonical or resonance structures, and the real molecule is a resonance hybrid, a single structure intermediate in energy and bond character between them — the molecule does not oscillate between the forms. Valid resonance structures must have the same positions of all atoms, the same number of paired and unpaired electrons, and comparable energy; only electron (bond/lone pair) positions differ. Resonance explains why, for example, all three N−O bonds in NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> are experimentally identical and intermediate in length between a single and a double bond, giving each bond a fractional bond order of 4/3. The contributing structure with formal charges closest to zero (and negative charge on the more electronegative atom) contributes most to the hybrid.
key_formulas: Average (resonance) bond order = total bond order summed over equivalent resonance structures ÷ number of structures
e.g. NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> and CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>: N−O / C−O bond order = 4/3; O<sub>3</sub>: O−O bond order = 3/2
topics.worked_example: Find the N−O bond order in NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>. It has 3 equivalent resonance structures, and in each one N−O bond is a double bond (order 2) while the other two are single bonds (order 1). Averaging over the 3 structures, each N−O bond order = (2+1+1)/3 = 4/3, which matches the single, intermediate bond length observed experimentally for all three bonds.
common_mistakes: Treating resonance as the molecule physically flipping between structures rather than one true hybrid
Drawing a 'resonance structure' that moves an atom instead of only moving electrons
Forgetting to divide by the number of contributing structures when computing average bond order

topics.name: Polarity of Bonds and Dipole Moment
topics.summary: A covalent bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar: the shared electron pair is displaced toward the more electronegative atom, creating a partial negative charge (δ−) there and a partial positive charge (δ+) on the other atom. Dipole moment (μ) quantifies this separation of charge as μ = q × d, where q is the magnitude of charge and d is the distance between charge centres; it is a vector, conventionally drawn from the positive to the negative end, measured in Debye (D). For polyatomic molecules the net (molecular) dipole moment is the vector sum of all individual bond dipoles, so a molecule with polar bonds can still be non-polar overall if its shape makes the bond dipoles cancel by symmetry (e.g. linear CO<sub>2</sub>, trigonal planar BF<sub>3</sub>, tetrahedral CCl<sub>4</sub>), while an asymmetric shape (bent H<sub>2</sub>O, pyramidal NH<sub>3</sub>) leaves a net non-zero dipole.
key_formulas: μ = q × d (measured in Debye, D)
Net molecular dipole moment = vector sum of all bond dipole moments
topics.worked_example: Explain why CO<sub>2</sub> has zero net dipole moment despite having two highly polar C=O bonds. CO<sub>2</sub> is linear (O=C=O, 180°), so the two equal and oppositely directed C=O bond dipoles point away from each other along the same line and cancel exactly, giving μ = 0 for the molecule as a whole, even though each individual C=O bond is strongly polar.
common_mistakes: Assuming a molecule with polar bonds must itself be polar, ignoring molecular geometry
Forgetting that dipole moment is a vector and adding bond dipole magnitudes without considering direction
Missing the effect of a lone pair's own dipole contribution (as in the NH<sub>3</sub> vs NF<sub>3</sub> anomaly)

topics.name: Fajans' Rules and Polarisation
topics.summary: Even a bond classified as 'ionic' usually has some covalent character, because the cation's electric field can distort (polarise) the anion's electron cloud, pulling shared density back toward itself. Fajans' rules state that covalent character in an otherwise ionic bond increases with: (1) smaller cation size (higher charge density, so greater polarising power), (2) larger anion size (more easily polarised, more diffuse electron cloud), and (3) higher charge on either ion. A special case is that cations with a pseudo-noble-gas (18-electron, e.g. Ag<sup>+</sup>, Cu<sup>+</sup>) configuration polarise anions more strongly than cations of similar size and charge with a true noble-gas (8-electron) configuration, because d-electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly. These rules explain why, for example, LiCl is markedly more covalent than NaCl or KCl, and why AlCl<sub>3</sub> and BeCl<sub>2</sub> behave as covalent, low-melting, sublimable compounds rather than typical ionic solids.
key_formulas: Covalent character ↑ as: cation size ↓, anion size ↑, ionic charge ↑
Pseudo-noble-gas cation (18 e<sup>−</sup>) > noble-gas cation (8 e<sup>−</sup>) in polarising power, size/charge held equal
topics.worked_example: Explain why AgCl is less ionic than NaCl despite Ag<sup>+</sup> and Na<sup>+</sup> having comparable ionic radii. Ag<sup>+</sup> has a pseudo-noble-gas (18-electron, [Kr]4d<sup>10</sup>) configuration whose d-electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly, giving it much greater polarising power than Na<sup>+</sup> (true 8-electron noble-gas configuration) of similar size. Ag<sup>+</sup> therefore polarises Cl<sup>−</sup> more strongly, giving AgCl significantly greater covalent character and a lower melting point than the size/charge comparison with NaCl alone would predict.
common_mistakes: Applying Fajans' rules using size and charge alone while ignoring pseudo-noble-gas configuration effects
Reversing the rule and thinking a larger cation increases covalent character
Confusing anion polarisability (favoured by large anion size) with cation polarising power (favoured by small cation size)

topics.name: VSEPR Theory and Molecular Shapes
topics.summary: The Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory predicts molecular shape by treating all electron pairs (bonding and lone) around a central atom as mutually repelling regions that arrange themselves as far apart as possible to minimise repulsion, with the repulsion order lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair. The total number of electron domains (steric number = number of sigma bonds/bonded atoms + number of lone pairs on the central atom; a multiple bond still counts as one domain) fixes the 'electron-pair geometry', while the 'molecular shape' is what remains after lone pairs are removed from the description — the two are the same only when there are no lone pairs on the central atom. Lone pairs occupy more space than bond pairs, so their presence compresses bond angles below the ideal value (CH<sub>4</sub> 109.5° > NH<sub>3</sub> 107° > H<sub>2</sub>O 104.5°).
key_formulas: Steric number = (number of atoms bonded to central atom) + (number of lone pairs on central atom)
SN 2 linear, SN 3 trigonal planar, SN 4 tetrahedral, SN 5 trigonal bipyramidal, SN 6 octahedral (electron-pair geometry)
topics.worked_example: Predict the shape of SF<sub>4</sub>. Sulfur is bonded to 4 F atoms and its Lewis structure leaves 1 lone pair on S, giving steric number 5 (electron-pair geometry: trigonal bipyramidal). The lone pair occupies an equatorial position (minimising 90° lp-bp repulsions), so the resulting molecular shape, once the lone pair is 'removed' from the description, is see-saw (irregular tetrahedron), not trigonal bipyramidal.
common_mistakes: Reporting the electron-pair geometry (which includes lone pairs) as the molecular shape
Forgetting that a double or triple bond still counts as only one electron domain for VSEPR purposes
Placing a lone pair axially instead of equatorially in trigonal bipyramidal cases, giving the wrong shape (e.g. for ClF<sub>3</sub>, SF<sub>4</sub>)

topics.name: Valence Bond Theory
topics.summary: Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains covalent bond formation as the overlap of atomic orbitals, each containing one unpaired electron, from two approaching atoms; bond strength increases with the extent of overlap. A sigma (σ) bond forms by head-on (axial) overlap along the internuclear axis (s−s, s−p, p−p, or hybrid orbital overlap) and permits free rotation about the bond axis. A pi (π) bond forms by sideways (lateral) overlap of unhybridised p orbitals lying parallel to each other and perpendicular to the internuclear axis; because this overlap is less effective than head-on overlap, π bonds are weaker than σ bonds and restrict free rotation, which is why cis/trans isomerism exists in alkenes but not alkanes. In a multiple bond, exactly one bond is σ and any additional bonds are π (double bond = 1σ+1π; triple bond = 1σ+2π).
key_formulas: Single bond = 1σ; Double bond = 1σ + 1π; Triple bond = 1σ + 2π
Overlap strength (bond strength): head-on (σ) > sideways (π)
topics.worked_example: Count the σ and π bonds in acetylene, H−C≡C−H. There are 2 C−H single bonds (2σ) and one C≡C triple bond, which is 1σ+2π. Total: 3σ bonds (2 C−H + 1 C−C) and 2π bonds, all from the one C≡C linkage.
common_mistakes: Counting a double bond as 2σ or a triple bond as 3σ instead of only one σ per multiple bond
Assuming π bonds are stronger than σ bonds because they are drawn as 'extra' lines
Forgetting that free rotation is restricted specifically by π bonds, not σ bonds

topics.name: Hybridisation
topics.summary: Hybridisation is the mixing of atomic orbitals of comparable energy on the same atom to form a new set of equivalent hybrid orbitals, which then overlap with other orbitals to form σ bonds or hold lone pairs; it explains observed molecular shapes and equal bond lengths/angles that simple unhybridised s and p orbitals cannot. The type of hybridisation is fixed by the steric number (number of σ bonds + lone pairs) at the central atom: sp (steric number 2, linear, 180°), sp<sup>2</sup> (3, trigonal planar, 120°), sp<sup>3</sup> (4, tetrahedral, 109.5°), sp<sup>3</sup>d (5, trigonal bipyramidal), sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> (6, octahedral), and sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>3</sup> (7, pentagonal bipyramidal, e.g. IF<sub>7</sub>). Only unhybridised orbitals (if any remain) are available to form π bonds, so a carbon with one π bond is sp<sup>2</sup> and a carbon with two π bonds (or a triple bond) is sp.
key_formulas: Hybridisation state determined by steric number: 2=sp, 3=sp<sup>2</sup>, 4=sp<sup>3</sup>, 5=sp<sup>3</sup>d, 6=sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>, 7=sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>3</sup>
Number of hybrid orbitals formed = number of atomic orbitals mixed
topics.worked_example: Find the hybridisation of Xe in XeF<sub>4</sub>. Xe forms 4 Xe−F σ bonds and its Lewis structure leaves 2 lone pairs on Xe, giving a steric number of 4 + 2 = 6. Steric number 6 corresponds to sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> hybridisation (octahedral electron-pair geometry), and with the 2 lone pairs placed opposite each other to minimise repulsion, the molecular shape is square planar.
common_mistakes: Counting only bonded atoms and forgetting to add lone pairs when finding the steric number
Assuming a double or triple bond adds extra hybrid orbitals instead of counting it as one σ-bond domain
Mislabelling hybridisation directly from molecular shape without first checking for lone pairs on the central atom

topics.name: Molecular Orbital Theory
topics.summary: Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT), developed by Hund and Mulliken, treats electrons in a molecule as occupying molecular orbitals formed by the Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals (LCAO) rather than remaining localised on individual atoms. In-phase (additive) combination of atomic orbitals gives a bonding MO, lower in energy than the parent atomic orbitals; out-of-phase (subtractive) combination gives an antibonding MO, higher in energy. Electrons fill molecular orbitals in order of increasing energy following the Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion principle, and Hund's rule, exactly as for atomic orbitals. For B<sub>2</sub>, C<sub>2</sub> and N<sub>2</sub> (Z ≤ 7) the σ2p<sub>z</sub> orbital lies above the π2p<sub>x,y</sub> orbitals due to s−p mixing, whereas for O<sub>2</sub>, F<sub>2</sub> and Ne<sub>2</sub> the σ2p<sub>z</sub> lies below the π2p<sub>x,y</sub> orbitals. Bond order, the number of bonds, is calculated from the electron populations, and MOT correctly predicts O<sub>2</sub>'s paramagnetism, which simple Lewis structures fail to explain.
key_formulas: Bond order = (N<sub>b</sub> − N<sub>a</sub>)/2, where N<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>a</sub> = electrons in bonding/antibonding MOs

Order for B<sub>2</sub>,C<sub>2</sub>,N<sub>2</sub>: σ2s,σ*2s,π2p<sub>x,y</sub>,σ2p<sub>z</sub>,π*2p<sub>x,y</sub>,σ*2p<sub>z</sub>; for O<sub>2</sub>,F<sub>2</sub>,Ne<sub>2</sub> swap σ2p<sub>z</sub> and π2p<sub>x,y</sub>
topics.worked_example: Find the bond order and magnetic nature of O<sub>2</sub> using MOT. O<sub>2</sub> has 12 valence electrons filling (σ2s)<sup>2</sup>(σ*2s)<sup>2</sup>(σ2p<sub>z</sub>)<sup>2</sup>(π2p<sub>x</sub>)<sup>2</sup>(π2p<sub>y</sub>)<sup>2</sup>(π*2p<sub>x</sub>)<sup>1</sup>(π*2p<sub>y</sub>)<sup>1</sup>. Bonding electrons = 8, antibonding = 4, so bond order = (8−4)/2 = 2. The two degenerate π* orbitals each hold one unpaired electron (Hund's rule), so O<sub>2</sub> is paramagnetic.
common_mistakes: Using the N<sub>2</sub>-type filling order (π below σ2p<sub>z</sub>) for O<sub>2</sub> or F<sub>2</sub>, or vice versa
Forgetting Hund's rule and pairing electrons in degenerate π*/π orbitals too early, misjudging magnetic behaviour
Leaving out core (1s) electrons inconsistently, or including them when only valence bond order is asked for

topics.name: Bonding in Homonuclear Diatomic Molecules
topics.summary: Applying Molecular Orbital Theory to the second-period homonuclear diatomics gives a clear trend: H<sub>2</sub> (bond order 1) and Li<sub>2</sub> (bond order 1) exist and are stable, but He<sub>2</sub> and Be<sub>2</sub> have bond order 0 (equal bonding and antibonding electrons) and do not exist as stable molecules. B<sub>2</sub> (bond order 1) is paramagnetic because its two π2p electrons singly occupy degenerate orbitals by Hund's rule. C<sub>2</sub> (bond order 2) is diamagnetic since both π2p orbitals are fully paired. N<sub>2</sub> (bond order 3) has the highest bond order of the series, is diamagnetic, and its very strong triple bond makes it exceptionally unreactive. O<sub>2</sub> (bond order 2) is paramagnetic due to two unpaired electrons in its π* orbitals — a result MOT predicts correctly but simple Lewis structures cannot. F<sub>2</sub> (bond order 1) is diamagnetic, and Ne<sub>2</sub> (bond order 0) does not exist. Removing or adding electrons from O<sub>2</sub> changes its bond order: O<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> (2.5) > O<sub>2</sub> (2) > O<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> (1.5) > O<sub>2</sub><sup>2−</sup> (1), with bond length increasing in that same order.
key_formulas: Bond order sequence, Li<sub>2</sub>→Ne<sub>2</sub>: 1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 0
For a given element, bond length ∝ 1/bond order (higher bond order = shorter, stronger bond)
topics.worked_example: Compare the stability of O<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>. O<sub>2</sub> has bond order 2 with 2 unpaired π* electrons. Removing one electron from an antibonding π* orbital to form O<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> raises the bond order to (8−3)/2 = 2.5, so O<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> has a shorter, stronger O−O bond than neutral O<sub>2</sub>, even though it has one fewer electron overall.
common_mistakes: Assuming removing an electron from any species always weakens its bond, without checking whether it left a bonding or antibonding orbital
Predicting C<sub>2</sub> is paramagnetic by wrongly applying the N<sub>2</sub>-type filling order inconsistently to magnetism

topics.name: Hydrogen Bonding
topics.summary: A hydrogen bond is a weak electrostatic attraction between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) and a lone pair on a nearby electronegative atom (F, O or N), either in another molecule (intermolecular H-bonding) or within the same molecule (intramolecular H-bonding). Intermolecular H-bonding causes molecules to associate, raising boiling point, viscosity and melting point above what molecular mass alone would predict — explaining the anomalously high boiling points of HF, H<sub>2</sub>O and NH<sub>3</sub> compared to the other hydrides in their respective groups (e.g. H<sub>2</sub>O >> H<sub>2</sub>S), and why para-nitrophenol (which forms intermolecular H-bonds and associates) has a higher boiling point and lower water solubility than ortho-nitrophenol (which forms an intramolecular H-bond instead, so it does not associate and is more volatile). Extensive H-bonding in ice creates an open, cage-like lattice, making ice less dense than liquid water and giving water its maximum density at 4°C.
key_formulas: H-bond requires: H−X covalent bond where X = F, O or N (small, highly electronegative)
Intermolecular H-bonding ↑ boiling point / viscosity; intramolecular H-bonding ↓ boiling point (no association)
topics.worked_example: Explain why NH<sub>3</sub> has a much higher boiling point than PH<sub>3</sub>. Nitrogen is small and highly electronegative, so N−H bonds in NH<sub>3</sub> support strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding, causing molecules to associate and raising the boiling point well above the trend for group 15 hydrides. Phosphorus is larger and far less electronegative, so P−H bonds in PH<sub>3</sub> cannot form significant hydrogen bonds, and PH<sub>3</sub> boils at a much lower temperature consistent with its molecular mass alone.
common_mistakes: Treating any H-containing bond as capable of hydrogen bonding, forgetting X must be F, O or N specifically
Confusing intramolecular H-bonding (lowers boiling point, no association) with intermolecular H-bonding (raises boiling point, causes association)
Missing that H-bonding, not just molecular mass, is the reason for anomalous trends within a hydride series
